title: Open Model Fit & Kernel Mapping — Catalog Strategy Demo
summary: Short demo showing how Redwood's model catalog surfaces open-model fit, latency/cost benchmarking, and a hardware/kernel compatibility matrix. AE covers business use cases and pricing signals; SE dives into kernel mapping, quantization tradeoffs, and suggested benchmark configs. Customer is interested in a short POC focused on latency-sensitive chat and a longer-throughput embed pipeline.

Diego to run a 10k-request P95 latency test on Stratus sample (by 2026-04-20)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Stratus Head of Platform), Ethan Morales (ML Eng), Sophie Li (Infra)
---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I'm Maya, account lead for Redwood Inference. Diego's our SE and he'll show the catalog and some kernel mapping details. Quick sanity check: is this still the 16:00 slot for roughly an hour?
[00:08] Priya Kapoor: Yep, works for us. Thanks Maya.
[00:11] Maya Chen: Cool. High-level agenda — quick product walkthrough of the model catalog, how we pick open models, our benchmark artifacts, then Diego will dig into the compatibility matrix and kernel/quantization notes. We'll close with recommended POC steps.
[00:25] Diego Alvarez: Hi all, Diego here. I'll share my screen in a sec — calling out up front that I'll get slightly nerdy on kernels and quantization, that seems relevant for the latency constraints you mentioned in the brief.
[00:34] Sophie Li: Yep, our infra is tight on latency — target p95 ~120ms for chat, but we also have an embedding pipeline that needs batched throughput. Two different profiles.
[00:45] Ethan Morales: And just to add, sample lengths are mixed: chat avg 250 tokens, some bursts 1024. So the sequence-length distribution matters.
[00:54] Maya Chen: Great context. Diego, over to you.
[01:00] Diego Alvarez: Ok screen up — this is the catalog UI. Top left you can filter by task, model family, latency bucket, and cost per 1k tokens. I'm going to switch to the "open models" view. Notice the scorecard for each model — accuracy proxy, median latency on H100/A100, and an entry called "compat matrix".
[01:23] Diego Alvarez: When you click compatibility, it expands into a table mapping model variant -> supported kernels -> recommended quantization profiles -> expected perf on common instance types. Quick example: a T5-like open model quantized to 4-bit using our Q4_K_M kernel shows a 2.8x speedup vs 8-bit on H100 for short sequences, but for 1k+ sequences the memory paging pattern changes and A100 with 8-bit can be cheaper.
[01:52] Ethan Morales: Wait, single question — Q4_K_M kernel, is that Redwood proprietary?
[01:56] Diego Alvarez: It's our optimized kernel selection — some kernels are third-party fused ops, others are our tuning of attention kernels. We label them generically in the UI as "Q4-fast" or "Q8-stable" to not expose implementations. It's not a black box for you — we provide perf numbers and fallback options.
[02:11] Priya Kapoor: How confident are those perf numbers? Are they from your internal traces or do you run them on customer-like workloads?
[02:18] Diego Alvarez: Good point. The catalog shows two columns: standardized microbenchmarks and a workspace for customer benchmarks. Microbenchmarks are stable across model versions and hardware; the "customer-run" column is where we put results from runs you trigger — same harness but with your sequences. So priya, we'll definitely recommend you run the 10k-sample P95 test we talked about.
[02:36] Sophie Li: Also curious about batching behavior — the embedding pipeline will want large batch sizes, but chat is low latency and we can't introduce 30–50ms queueing.
[02:46] Diego Alvarez: Right. We support mixed serving modes: immediate priority lanes for chat (tiny batch/eviction-friendly KV cache) and throughput lanes for bulk embeddings (larger batching windows). The runtime automatically routes by policy — you can pin endpoints to either lane or let our smart router do it. It adapts to latency SLOs.
[03:03] Maya Chen: Diego, perhaps show a quick compatibility example between H100 and a more cost-conscious 80GB A100 setup?
[03:10] Diego Alvarez: Sure — flipping to the matrix. Here we have Model-A (a LLaMA-style 13B open model). On H100 with Q4-fast kernel we hit p50 ~28ms token generation for 250-token sequences and p95 ~110ms, whereas on A100 with Q8-stable it's slightly slower p95 ~150ms, but cost per token is 20% lower for batch-heavy workloads. There's a third column suggesting a quantization fallback: if you need lower tail latency, use an H100 pool and the Q4 kernel; if cost-sensitive, A100 + Q8 gives better unit economics.
[03:43] Ethan Morales: Those p95 numbers — are they end-to-end including network from our VPC peering or just local runtime?
[03:48] Diego Alvarez: Good catch. The catalog numbers are runtime-only, not including customer network egress/ingress. For private deployments (VPC or dedicated) we run the benchmark in an environment that mirrors your networking and include end-to-end numbers in the customer-run workspace.
[04:03] Priya Kapoor: Security — does the customer-run workspace store my sample sequences? We can't have logs persisted in a shared bucket.
[04:10] Diego Alvarez: By default, the customer-run workspace is tenant isolated and ephemeral by default. For Hosted API runs we retain logs per your retention policy; for Dedicated or Private we provide options to keep them only in your VPC or not persist at all. We have KMS integrations and can use HSM-backed key wrapping for model keys and audit logs.
[04:28] Sophie Li: And SSO/SCIM for RBAC?
[04:31] Maya Chen: Yes, SAML and OIDC supported, SCIM provisioning, and per-token RBAC. We'll include the SOC2 documentation in the follow-up packet.
[04:40] Diego Alvarez: Back to the catalog — there's also a 'delta' column that shows relative quality regressions when moving to smaller quantization. For example, for a summarization metric Model-A loses ~1.2 Rouge if you go Q4 aggressively; for conversational intent tasks the delta is often smaller. The playbook recommends a small eval set per task.
[05:01] Ethan Morales: Can you show the benchmarking config we should run?
[05:05] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely — clicking "benchmark template". It prepopulates sequence distribution (percentiles), batch sizes, kernel selection, and a warmup schedule. We recommend 2k warmup requests, then a 10k steady-state run for p95 accuracy. Warmup helps the KV cache and JIT kernels stabilize.
[05:26] Priya Kapoor: Is there a recommended sampling for chat logs? We can't send PII.
[05:29] Diego Alvarez: We usually accept an anonymized sample — you can redact or hash user ids. If there's regulated data, we suggest running the private deployment POC where data never leaves your VPC.
[05:39] Maya Chen: Quick pricing note — Hosted API pricing vs Dedicated reserved capacity: Hosted is easiest to start and we can show per-token cost for each kernel/hardware in the catalog. Dedicated has upfront commit but predictable throughput and lower marginal cost. We'll put the pricing breakouts in the sheet.
[05:58] Sophie Li: For Dedicated, do you support our existing cluster manager? We run Nomad + custom autoscaler.
[06:03] Diego Alvarez: We integrate at the control-plane level; Dedicated nodes can be managed by us or we can export a deployment artifact you run inside Nomad. There are setup differences for autoscaling; we usually co-design a handshake.
[06:15] Ethan Morales: Any mention of model rollout/versions?
[06:18] Diego Alvarez: Yes — the console has model pinning and rollout controls. You can canary a new model variant to a small % of traffic; if quality drops we auto-fallback to a pinned previous variant. The compatibility matrix is versioned per model so you can see kernel compatibility across model releases.
[06:35] Priya Kapoor: Can we force particular kernels? Our compliance team wants deterministic behavior.
[06:39] Diego Alvarez: You can pin kernel + quantization profile at the route level in the config — that ensures deterministic serving. We also expose kernel-level logging if you want traces.
[06:49] Maya Chen: Quick question from our side — what's your expected time to set up a short POC if Stratus provides sample data?
[06:55] Diego Alvarez: For Hosted POC with your sample and configured benchmarks we can run initial results in 48–72 hours. For Dedicated or Private it's typically 2–4 weeks due to infra/provisioning and security review.
[07:07] Sophie Li: 2–4 weeks for Private OK. We may start Hosted to iterate.
[07:12] Diego Alvarez: Perfect. Let me demo a couple kernel tradeoffs visually — switching to the kernel trace view.
[07:20] Diego Alvarez: The trace shows, for a mid-length request, attention kernel time vs token-matrix multiply. For some open models, fused attention kernels reduce memory copies, which improves p50 by 30ms but at the cost of longer warmup JIT; that's why we recommend warmup. Also, prefix caching/KV cache behavior: for chat, the KV cache avoids re-computing previous context — in our runtime we have an eviction heuristic tuned for low-latency lanes.
[07:49] Ethan Morales: Do you support offloading KV cache to system memory or NVMe? We have constrained GPU memory on some nodes.
[07:53] Diego Alvarez: Yes — we support asynchronous KV spilling to host memory and NVMe-backed shards. There's a perf vs cost trade: spilling reduces GPU memory pressure but can increase tail latency. The compatibility matrix signals when a model+kernel pair is KV-friendly.
[08:10] Priya Kapoor: Any recommended quantization for embeddings? We want 512-d vectors, accuracy matters more than tiny savings.
[08:15] Diego Alvarez: For embeddings we typically recommend 8-bit quantization unless your eval shows quality degradation. Embedding quality tends to be sensitive to aggressive 4-bit for some model families. The catalog has embedding-specific deltas.
[08:27] Maya Chen: I'll pause here — quick check: are there any blocking security or compliance asks we should address right away?
[08:33] Priya Kapoor: SOC2 + SAML + KMS integration are must-haves. Also need a clear retention and deletion policy for any sample logs.
[08:41] Maya Chen: We'll include SOC2 attestation, SSO integration docs, KMS architecture, and the retention configs in the follow-up package.
[08:48] Sophie Li: One more infra ask — can your routing fall back across regions if capacity constrained? We need multi-region failover.
[08:54] Diego Alvarez: Yes — the routing layer supports region-aware fallbacks and model-variant fallbacks. You can set policy order: region -> model-variant -> cost-tier. It will try to respect data residency settings.
[09:06] Ethan Morales: Any experience with long-context models? We have periodic tasks that require 8k contexts.
[09:11] Diego Alvarez: We support long-context variants; the compatibility matrix highlights memory growth and kernel support for >4k sequences. For >8k sometimes a different attention kernel or chunked-processing pattern is suggested.
[09:26] Priya Kapoor: Ok, want to talk timeline — we want a quick Hosted POC to validate latency for chat and a dedicated throughput pilot for embeddings. Can you propose a minimal success criteria?
[09:35] Maya Chen: Sure — suggested success criteria: 1) Hosted POC: p95 chat latency <= 130ms on 95% of test runs with anonymized sample; 2) Embedding pilot: 5M embeddings/day with cost per embed below X (we'll provide baseline); 3) Quality gates: minimal delta vs your current embed model (<1% recall loss). Diego, we'll map config.
[09:56] Diego Alvarez: I'll add config: chat bench: 2k warmup, 10k steady-state, seq distribution as provided; embed bench: batched runs with batch sizes 256/512 to match your pipeline. We'll include kernel pin examples and a fallback policy.
[10:12] Ethan Morales: Sounds good. A question on audit logs — do logs include request traces or only coarse metrics?
[10:17] Diego Alvarez: Both options. By default we provide token-level cost metrics and event-level traces; request payloads are redacted unless you opt-in to full tracing. Audit logs are immutable and can be exported to your SIEM via syslog or S3; in Private they never leave your network.
[10:31] Priya Kapoor: Great. Are there any known gotchas for migrating from our current Triton infra?
[10:35] Diego Alvarez: Triton is great for standard model serving; the main differences are runtime batching and KV caching semantics. We provide a migration playbook that covers model packaging (hf format conversion), quantization recommended steps, and kernel compatibility checks. We'll share it.
[10:48] Maya Chen: Quick time check — about 40 minutes left? We're at ~10 min marker in recording? Actually this was a long opener, we still have plenty of time — but let's jump to Q&A then wrap with next steps.
[11:00] Priya Kapoor: One more thing on cost modeling — can the catalog show a simulated monthly bill given our traffic profile?
[11:07] Diego Alvarez: Yes — the catalog has a 'cost simulator' where you input traffic profile (rps, avg seq len, batch targets) and it shows cost across hardware + kernel choices and a recommended hybrid routing that minimizes expected spend while meeting latency SLOs. We can run your profile once you give the sample.
[11:27] Ethan Morales: Do you provide tokenization parity? We use an internal tokenizer variant that sometimes changes token counts by ~3–4% which affects cost estimates.
[11:33] Diego Alvarez: We can accept your tokenizer binary or a small sample; the benchmark harness will use it. That will give more accurate token counts.
[11:41] Sophie Li: Any public-facing benchmarks where we can compare models side-by-side?
[11:44] Diego Alvarez: The catalog has curated benchmark pages. We publish standardized bench suites (latency, throughput, embedding recall) for each model variant. For confidentiality we show relative deltas for some closed-source models.
[11:56] Priya Kapoor: Ok let's go through immediate next steps quickly.
[12:00] Maya Chen: I'll recap: Maya will send pricing and the benchmark template by Friday 2026-04-16; Diego will run the initial 10k perf run within a week of us receiving the sample dataset and share kernel traces; Priya will provide anonymized sample and expected SLOs by Friday. We'll tentatively schedule POC kickoff for week of 2026-04-27; if Dedicated needed we'll start infra provisioning separately. Any objections?
[12:23] Priya Kapoor: No objections, sounds good.
[12:26] Ethan Morales: All good.
[12:28] Maya Chen: Perfect — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite and the materials.
---
End of transcript (some stutters and mislabels as typical with AI transcript; speaker boundaries approximate).
